summary: An Imaginary Cloud blog article by Alex Gamela, last updated November 24, 2023, that introduces Julia as a fast, math-oriented language and compares it with Python, which it uses as a reference. It covers each language's origins and main features, differences in popularity, name origin, data science, machine learning, integration, speed and compilation, and gives a comparison table. It concludes that the better choice depends on the task, with Julia favored for numerical and scientific computing and Python for its large ecosystem.
one_line: A blog comparison of Julia and Python covering origins, features, speed, ecosystem, naming history, and suitability for data science and machine learning.
key_facts: Python was introduced in 1991 and is described as a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose, multi-paradigm language.
Julia was created in 2012 and got its first stable release in 2018.
Julia is described as a dynamic, high-level, high-performance programming language specifically created for technical computing.
Julia uses the LLVM framework and compiles code to machine code at runtime (JIT).
Julia allows the use of Greek letters, enabling direct use of mathematical formulas in code.
The name 'Python' derives from 'Monty Python's Flying Circus', the BBC comedy series from the 1970s.
Guido van Rossum was reading the show's published scripts when he started developing Python.
Julia's name was suggested once during a casual conversation to Alan Edelman as a good name for a programming language.
At the time of writing, Python was leading the Tiobe Index while Julia stood at number 36.
NumPy is named as the external library Python needs for statistical and advanced math work.
Julia can call libraries from Fortran, C, or Python and can interface directly with Python to share data.
The article states that Julia is only beaten by C in speed.
The article says Julia is designed for parallel computing at every level, including instruction-level parallelism, multi-threading, GPU computing, and distributed computing.
The article concludes that the better choice between Julia and Python depends on the specific task and project requirements.
The article states that more than 500,000 people read the Imaginary Cloud blog every year.
